techniques: audience positioning; brand loyalty; mode of address
paragraph: This new, limited edition bag of Crunchers crisps has a large badge on the front that says, "You chose this flavour!" Last summer, the brand asked the public to vote online between three new flavours, and more than a million people took part in just two weeks. The winning flavour, chilli and lime, is shown in a packshot with a bright green and red background. On the back, the body copy thanks fans for voting and invites them to suggest next year's flavour on the brand's website or social media.

advert: Root & Branch soap: brown paper, string, and a paragraph on the brand's values
paragraph: This bar of Root & Branch soap is wrapped in plain brown paper and tied with natural string. There is no plastic anywhere on the packaging. A small paper label shows a simple hand-drawn tree. On the back, a short paragraph explains the brand's values: every ingredient is grown on small farms, nothing is tested on animals, and ten per cent of profits support forest projects. The language is simple and personal, ending with the words, "Thank you for choosing gently." The bar costs £7, much more than ordinary soap.

advert: Regent saloon car: an older man drives slowly to piano music
paragraph: This TV advert for the Regent saloon car shows a grey-haired man in his sixties driving slowly along a coastal road at sunset. Gentle piano music plays. He is alone in the car, relaxed and smiling slightly, with one hand on the wheel. The car's interior is shown in close-up: soft leather seats, wooden panels and a quiet engine. There is no talk of speed or price. At the end, a calm male voice says, "The Regent. You've arrived." The advert is shown during evening news programmes and golf tournaments.

advert: Wave mobile network: casual teen language and invented words
techniques: mode of address; neologism; target audience
paragraph: This magazine advert for the Wave mobile network is aimed at teenagers. It shows three friends taking a selfie together on a city rooftop at night, all laughing. The text is written as if it were a text message between friends: "No cap, Wave is lowkey the best deal rn." Below this, the body copy uses invented words such as "datastic" and "unlimitless" to describe the new unlimited phone plan. The price, £12 a month, is printed in a speech bubble, along with the line, "Ur parents will approve too."

advert: Quit Now: a cigarette shown as a burning fuse
paragraph: This poster for the Quit Now campaign shows a single cigarette on a black background. However, the cigarette looks like the fuse of a bomb: the end is burning with bright orange sparks, and a thin line of smoke rises above it. There are no people or other objects in the image. Below the picture, white letters say, "Every cigarette brings it closer." Underneath, in smaller letters, there is the number of a free, confidential helpline. The posters appear on the sides of city buses and in hospital waiting rooms.

advert: A countdown timer, "Offer ends in 09:59", that restarts when the page reloads
paragraph: When a customer visits the website of Trendy, an online clothes shop, a bright pop-up appears immediately with a red countdown timer: "Offer ends in 09:59." The pop-up promises 40% off absolutely everything if the customer orders before the timer reaches zero. The numbers tick down second by second, and a message underneath says, "23 people are looking at this item right now." However, if the customer reloads the page, the timer starts again from ten minutes. Several consumer groups have already complained about the website to the advertising regulator.

advert: A health page article about Vita vitamin gummies
paragraph: This page in a weekend newspaper looks like a normal health article. Its headline asks, "Are you getting enough vitamins this winter?" The article interviews a nutrition expert and describes how tiredness, low mood and colds are common in the dark winter months. Near the end, it recommends Vita gummies, describing them as "the easy way to stay healthy". A photo shows the colourful, fruit-shaped sweets in a glass bowl. At the bottom, small text says "Advertisement feature", and a line warns that supplements should not replace a varied diet.

advert: Lumi perfume: a short film with no words at all
techniques: soft sell; lifestyle advertising; brand identity
paragraph: This two-minute TV advert for Lumi perfume is like a short film. A young woman runs through the streets of Paris at night, past glowing cafés and shop windows, across a bridge and up the stairs of an old building. She opens a door onto a rooftop full of light and music, where a group of friends welcome her. Nobody speaks, and we never learn her story. The perfume bottle is not shown until the final three seconds, when it appears on a black screen with the single word "Lumi".

advert: Sterling Cars: "0% finance! Today only!" in red
paragraph: This billboard for Sterling Cars is bright red and covered in large yellow letters. The main headline shouts, "0% finance! Today only!" Below it, three new cars are shown with huge prices beside them, and a starburst shape says, "Huge savings!" A huge arrow points down the road towards the garage, which is only two hundred metres away. At the bottom, in very small white text, a disclaimer explains that the offer depends on a large first payment and is only available to some customers with a good credit history.

advert: Gym adverts appear after several late-night fast food orders
paragraph: After a young man orders fast food from a delivery app late at night several times in one week, he begins to see adverts for the FitHouse gym on his phone. One shows a fit man of his age running at dawn and says, "Tired of feeling tired?" Another shows a pair of jeans that no longer fit around the waist, with the line, "It's not too late to start." The adverts appear mostly after midnight. Each one offers a free first week and a button that says "Start tomorrow".

advert: A footballer as brand ambassador for Aurum watches, with body copy about his career
paragraph: This magazine advert for Aurum watches shows a famous international footballer in a dark suit, sitting alone in an empty stadium at night, under the floodlights. He is looking down at the gold watch on his wrist and smiling slightly to himself. Under the photo, a paragraph of body copy describes his career: how he started playing on the streets of Lagos and became the captain of his national team. It ends with the line, "Every great moment is timed. Aurum." There is no price, only the brand's website address.

advert: Fairway Bank's new logo: lowercase letters and a smile
techniques: rebrand; mode of address; brand values
paragraph: This poster introduces the new look of Fairway Bank, which has been a traditional, serious bank for over a hundred years. The old dark blue shield has gone. In its place, the name "fairway" is written in round, lowercase letters, and the "y" curves upwards like a smile. The background is bright yellow, and the logo looks almost like a cartoon. The new strapline says, "Banking that's on your side." Underneath, the body copy explains that the bank's app has been redesigned to be simpler and friendlier for young customers.

advert: Hollins supermarket Christmas: families of every kind share one meal
paragraph: This Christmas TV advert for Hollins supermarket shows many different families preparing one meal in their own homes: a grandmother teaching her grandson to roast potatoes, two dads decorating a table, a student cooking for friends in a tiny flat, and a large Indian family making dessert. Warm, gentle music plays, and the camera moves smoothly from kitchen to kitchen. At the end, the screen splits, and all the families appear around their tables at the same time. The strapline appears in gold letters: "However you celebrate, Hollins is there."

advert: A Volt cola billboard inside a racing game
techniques: native advertising; target audience; brand identity
paragraph: In a popular car racing video game, players drive through a city at night at very high speed, avoiding traffic and the police. Along the road, there are huge, bright digital billboards for Volt cola, showing the red can and the brand's logo. When players pass a certain point, a Volt cola truck drives across the road. The billboards fit naturally into the game's world, and many players hardly notice them. The game is mainly played by teenagers and young adults, and it is completely free to download on phones.

advert: MaxBuild protein: an airbrushed male model and "Gains guaranteed"
paragraph: This magazine advert for MaxBuild protein powder shows a man with no shirt standing in a gym. His muscles are huge and perfectly defined, and his skin is smooth and shining under strong lights. The headline says, "Gains guaranteed. Results in 30 days." A large black tub of powder stands on a bench beside him, with gold letters on the label. Next to a star at the bottom of the page, small print explains that results depend on exercise and diet. Experts say the photo has clearly been digitally changed.

advert: EaseAll pain tablets: "Always read the label"
paragraph: This radio advert for EaseAll pain tablets begins with a tired woman sighing loudly, then describing a terrible headache that stopped her from working. A calm male voice explains that EaseAll contains ibuprofen and starts working in just fifteen minutes. He gives a few simple facts: suitable for adults, available in all chemists and supermarkets, and gentle on the stomach. At the end, he says clearly, "Always read the label. If symptoms continue, speak to your pharmacist." The final words are spoken slowly, so that every listener can hear them.

advert: Crunchtastic cereal: the made-up word sung again and again
paragraph: This TV advert for Crunchtastic cereal shows a family of colourful cartoon animals dancing around a kitchen table. A loud, catchy song plays, and the word "Crunchtastic" is sung again and again by different characters: the dog, the cat and even the talking toaster. Each time the word is sung, it appears in bright yellow letters on the screen. Then real children and parents are shown eating the cereal together at a sunny table and laughing. The advert is shown at breakfast time and during family programmes in the evening.

advert: Bright Energy: a simple chart of bills falling year by year
paragraph: This poster for Bright Energy shows a large, simple bar chart on a white background. The bars show a typical family's electricity bill falling year by year after switching to solar panels: from £1,200 to £400. The chart is in calm shades of green and blue. Under the chart, the caption says, "This is what switching looks like." A short paragraph explains that the panels are installed in one day and come with a twenty-year guarantee. The brand's values, "clean, simple, fair", appear in small letters next to the logo.

advert: A host sells face masks: "3, 2, 1, link's live!"
techniques: hard sell; scarcity; mode of address
paragraph: In a livestream on a Chinese shopping app, a popular host sits in a bright pink studio surrounded by boxes of face masks. She speaks extremely quickly, holding up the product and applying one to her own face. Every few minutes she shouts, "Only five thousand left! Three, two, one, link's live!" The number of buyers flashes on the screen, rising rapidly. Comments from viewers scroll past quickly, many asking about prices and skin types. The host calls viewers "family" and promises a free gift to the first thousand customers.

advert: Ridgeback 4x4: a lone driver crosses a desert
paragraph: This TV advert for the Ridgeback 4x4 shows a single driver crossing a huge, empty desert. There are no roads, only sand dunes, rocks and an enormous sky. The car climbs steep hills and races through a dry riverbed, sending up clouds of dust. At night, the driver sleeps on the roof under the stars. We never see a city, a road sign or another person during the whole advert. The strapline appears at the end: "Ridgeback. Go where the road ends." The advert appears during adventure and wildlife documentaries.

advert: A giant cartoon cat seems to climb out of the screen above a crossing
techniques: viral marketing; guerrilla marketing; brand identity
paragraph: Above a busy crossing in a large city, a giant curved screen shows a 3D image of a huge orange cartoon cat. Because of the shape of the screen, the cat appears to climb out of the building and look down at the people below. It yawns, stretches and finally holds up a can of Purr cat food. There are no words or prices, only the brand's logo in the corner. People stop in the street to film it, and videos of the billboard have been shared millions of times.

advert: Run Club sportswatch: a woman running alone in the rain; "Your pace"
techniques: anchorage; mode of address; brand values
paragraph: This poster for the Run Club sportswatch shows a woman running alone along an empty city street in heavy rain. She is soaking wet, but her face is calm and focused. On her wrist, the small watch screen is glowing bright green. The photo is dark, with grey and blue tones. The only words are "Your pace." in small white letters in the top corner, and the brand's logo below. The poster appears in train stations in the early morning, when tired commuters walk past on the way to work.

advert: Northern Oil: wind turbines and green leaves, with solar power mentioned in one line
paragraph: This full-page magazine advert for Northern Oil is dominated by green. A row of white wind turbines stands on a hillside covered in fresh grass, and in the foreground, a child's hand holds a single bright green leaf. The headline reads, "Powering a cleaner tomorrow." The body copy describes the company's investment in renewable energy, using words such as "natural", "responsible" and "future". Only one line, near the end, mentions that solar and wind make up less than three per cent of the company's business. The company's logo, a green and yellow sunflower, sits quietly in the bottom right corner.

advert: A parody of a burger chain's advert with a rewritten slogan about health
paragraph: This poster appeared overnight on a busy bus shelter in central London. At first glance, it looks exactly like an advert for Tasty Burger, with the same red background, the same smiling logo and the same photograph of a huge, dripping cheeseburger. However, the slogan has been changed from "Grab some happy" to "Grab some heart disease". Underneath, in the brand's own font, a line of small print lists the burger's salt, sugar and fat content. The poster was made by an activist group, not the company, and photos of it spread quickly across social media within a single day.

advert: Robo mop: a messy kitchen, a problem, a demonstration, then "Order now"
techniques: AIDA model; call to action; rational appeal
paragraph: This thirty-second TV advert for the Robo mop opens with a loud crash as a toddler knocks a bowl of cereal onto a clean white kitchen floor. The parents look at each other in complete despair. A voiceover asks, "Tired of cleaning the same floor three times a day?" Next, the Robo mop glides out from under a cupboard and cleans the mess in seconds while the family sit down to breakfast. The voiceover lists three features: it maps the room, it empties itself and it is controlled by a phone app. The final screen says, "Order now. Delivery tomorrow."

advert: Volley sportswear: girls' football team; "Play like a girl" as praise
paragraph: This TV advert for Volley sportswear follows a girls' under-fifteen football team through a muddy, rainy season. We see them training in the dark, arguing with referees and celebrating a very late winning goal. At the beginning, a boy on the touchline shouts, "You play like a girl!" as an insult. At the end, the team captain turns to the camera after scoring and repeats the phrase proudly: "Yeah. I play like a girl." The Volley logo appears on the team's shirts throughout, and the final screen shows the hashtag #LikeAGirl next to a link to the new women's collection.

advert: Kite phone: last year's model looks slow and dull beside the new one
paragraph: This TV advert for the new Kite phone uses a split screen. On the left, a young man struggles with last year's Kite 7 model: the screen is dull, apps load slowly and the battery runs out during a video call. The colours on that side are grey and washed out. On the right, a confident young woman uses the new model, which is bright, fast and full of colour, as she films a crowded outdoor concert. A voiceover says, "Why live in the past?" The final screen shows the new phone next to a trade-in offer for older models.

advert: Aurum watch: a man at dinner, his gold watch visible to every guest
paragraph: This magazine advert for Aurum shows a long dinner table in an elegant restaurant, lit by candles. Eight well-dressed guests in their thirties are laughing and talking. In the centre of the image, a man reaches for his wine glass, and his heavy gold watch catches the light. Several guests are glancing at it. The man's face is not fully shown, so the watch is the real subject of the photograph. The text is minimal: "Aurum. Noticed." There is no price and no information about the watch's features, only the brand name and the address of its single London boutique.

advert: Peak Air: cans of "fresh mountain air" for city buyers
paragraph: This online advert for Peak Air shows a small aluminium can with a picture of snowy mountains on the side. A young woman in a crowded, polluted city lifts the can to her face, presses a button and breathes in deeply. Her eyes close in pleasure, and she smiles slowly. The text describes the product as "100% pure Alpine air, hand-collected at 3,000 metres". It claims the air will leave buyers feeling "refreshed, focused and alive". Each can contains about one hundred breaths and costs £14.99. The advert appears on social media in cities with high levels of air pollution.

advert: Lumi perfume in the style of a black-and-white 1950s Hollywood film
paragraph: This TV advert for Lumi perfume is filmed entirely in black and white, in the style of a 1950s Hollywood film. A woman in a long satin dress and white gloves walks slowly down a grand marble staircase as an orchestra plays dramatic music. Men in dinner suits turn to watch her. The credits at the beginning use old-fashioned curly lettering, and the picture even has small scratches, as if it were an old film reel. In the final seconds, the bottle of Lumi appears in full colour, glowing gold, while the rest of the screen stays black and white.

advert: Homeguard alarms: a family sleeps safely while the house is protected
techniques: hierarchy of needs (safety); fear appeal; mode of address
paragraph: This TV advert for Homeguard alarm systems shows a family's house at night, seen from outside. Rain is falling, and a heavy storm is building. Inside, the parents check on their sleeping children before going to bed themselves. A small blue light glows steadily on a white box by the front door. A calm, reassuring voiceover says, "Whatever happens outside, they're safe inside." The camera then shows a phone screen, where the parents can watch every room. The advert ends with the family having breakfast together in a bright kitchen and the strapline, "Homeguard. Peace of mind, around the clock."

advert: Kingdom Clash: friends shout and laugh together on a video call
techniques: uses and gratifications (social interaction); bandwagon; target audience
paragraph: This online advert for Kingdom Clash does not show the game itself for most of its thirty seconds. Instead, it shows four teenage friends in different cities, each in their own bedroom, talking and laughing on a video call while they play together. One friend has just moved to a new country, and the others greet her with cheers when she joins their team. They share inside jokes and call each other by nicknames that only they understand. Only at the end does the advert show the game's colourful battle screen, followed by the line, "Wherever you are, play together."

advert: A subscription offer whose "no" button reads "No thanks, I don't like saving money"
paragraph: When readers try to leave the website of a popular food magazine, a large pop-up suddenly fills the screen. It offers a subscription at £1 for the first month. The "Subscribe" button is large, bright green and in the centre of the box. Underneath, in small grey text, the option to close the pop-up says, "No thanks, I don't like saving money." Next to the green button, a small box has already been ticked for them to agree to marketing emails. In the small print, readers can see that after the first month the price rises to £12 a month.

advert: Bean There: "The best coffee in the world"
paragraph: This billboard for Bean There coffee shows a close-up of a cup of coffee on a wooden table, with steam rising and a perfect heart drawn in the milk foam. Dark roasted coffee beans are scattered around the cup, and a small chocolate sits on the saucer. Across the top, in large, elegant cream letters, the billboard claims, "The best coffee in the world." There is no evidence, award or statistic to support the claim. Underneath, a smaller line reads, "Now in over 400 cafés." The billboard is placed directly opposite a rival coffee chain on a busy shopping street.

advert: Starlight jewellers: a red rose, a candle and a ring on a dark table
paragraph: This magazine advert for Starlight jewellers shows a dark wooden table lit only by a single candle. On the table, there is a single deep red rose and a small open box containing a diamond ring. A few rose petals lie beside it, and a glass of champagne stands in the shadows behind. The image is warm and slightly blurred at the edges, so the ring is the sharpest object in the picture. There are no people and no words except the brand's name, written in thin silver handwriting at the bottom, and the date of Valentine's Day, 14 February.

advert: Hollins supermarket: the same wealthy family in a large house in every advert
paragraph: Across a whole year of TV adverts, Hollins supermarket always uses the same family. The parents are white and in their forties, with two children, a boy and a girl, and a golden retriever. They live in a large detached house with a big garden in the countryside. The mother is usually cooking, while the father lights the barbecue or carves the meat. They are always calm and well-dressed, they never argue, and their huge kitchen is spotless and full of expensive equipment. Each advert ends with the family around the table and the strapline, "Hollins. Food for every family."

advert: Activists repaint a sale billboard to read "Buy more. Be happy?"
paragraph: This billboard originally advertised a huge three-day weekend sale at a shopping centre, with the headline "Buy more. Save more." and a photograph of smiling shoppers carrying bags. During the night, however, someone painted over two words, so that it now reads "Buy more. Be happy?" A large red question mark has been added beside the shoppers' smiling faces. The change was made by an anti-consumerism group, who also attached small stickers reading "Buy Nothing Day" around the frame. Photos of the altered billboard were shared thousands of times online before the shopping centre had it cleaned the next afternoon.

advert: Rocket crisps retell a famous fairy tale: the wolf only wants the crisps
paragraph: This TV advert for Rocket crisps retells the story of Little Red Riding Hood. A girl in a red cloak walks through a dark, misty forest, carrying a basket of food for her sick grandmother. When she reaches her grandmother's cottage, the wolf is in the bed, wearing a nightdress. However, when she says, "What big teeth you have!", the wolf ignores her and grabs the bag of Rocket crisps from her basket. He eats them noisily and happily and says, "Sorry, I'm not here for you." The advert ends with a packshot and the line, "Rocket. Worth the trip."

advert: Black Friday: crowds run through doors as a clock counts down
paragraph: This TV advert for ValueMart's Black Friday sale begins with a crowd of people waiting outside a large store in the dark. A large digital clock counts down the final seconds to midnight. When the doors open, the shoppers rush inside, grabbing televisions, laptops and toys from the shelves. Loud, upbeat music plays, and the editing is fast and exciting. Prices with red lines through them flash across the screen, replaced by lower ones. The voiceover shouts, "Biggest deals of the year! Once they're gone, they're gone!" The advert ends with smiling customers carrying huge cardboard boxes to their cars.

This online advert for Trendy's new "Conscious Collection" shows models in soft beige and green clothes walking through a sunny field of tall wild flowers. Leaves and small birds appear in the corners of the screen. Calm, elegant text across the screen says, "Fashion that cares for the planet." The collection is presented on a special green page of the website, with a leaf symbol beside each item. However, the product labels show that most items contain only 1% recycled cotton. The rest of the website continues to sell hundreds of brand new styles every week at very low prices.

advert: Ridgeback SUV in a city street; people turn to admire the owner
techniques: conspicuous consumption; hierarchy of needs (esteem); aspirational
paragraph: This TV advert for the Ridgeback SUV shows a large black car driving slowly down a busy, narrow city street. People on the pavement stop and turn to look at it. A group of young men nod in admiration, and a woman in a café smiles at the driver through the window. The driver, a man in his forties wearing dark sunglasses, parks in front of an expensive restaurant, and the doorman opens his door. The car never leaves the city, drives on rough ground or carries anything heavier than a shopping bag. The strapline appears: "Ridgeback. Make an entrance."

advert: Spark dating app: "Be the person you want to be"
techniques: uses and gratifications (personal identity); mode of address; commodification
paragraph: This online advert for the Spark dating app shows a series of short scenes of young people getting ready to go out: choosing clothes, practising a smile in the mirror, and taking a deep breath before entering a bar. Each person looks nervous and unsure at first, but calm and confident by the end of the scene. A voiceover says, "Be the person you want to be. Spark will help you find someone who loves them." Users' profile photos appear on screen, with descriptions such as "adventurous" and "creative". The advert ends with the line, "Your best self is waiting."

advert: A Fairway Bank campaign told in four posters along a corridor
paragraph: In a long corridor at a busy metro station, Fairway Bank has placed four posters in a row. The first shows only a large question: "Still paying bank fees?" The second shows a frustrated young woman looking at a bank charge on her phone. The third explains, in a few short lines, that Fairway's new account has no fees and pays interest every month. The fourth shows the same woman smiling, with the words, "Switch in ten minutes. Scan here." Each poster uses the same yellow background, and commuters see all four in order as they walk to the platform.

advert: Edge razors for women show real body hair
paragraph: This TV advert for Edge's women's razors shows women of different ages, ethnicities and body shapes at the beach, at the gym and in the bathroom. Unlike most razor adverts, it shows real, natural body hair on legs, arms and underarms. Some women shave, while others choose not to, and neither choice is shown as better. A voiceover says, "Your body. Your choice. No judgement." There is no slow motion, no perfect lighting and no models with already smooth legs. The final screen shows the razor in simple pink and grey packaging, alongside the words, "Edge. For whatever you decide."

advert: Homeguard insurance parodies a superhero film trailer
paragraph: This TV advert for Homeguard insurance is filmed like a trailer for a superhero film. Loud, dramatic orchestral music builds, and a deep voice says, "In a world of burst pipes and broken windows, one hero stands ready." A man in an ordinary grey suit, holding a clipboard, walks in slow motion away from a small kitchen flood while sparks fly behind him. He arrives at a family's door and says, "Don't worry, I'm from Homeguard." The title appears in huge metal letters: "HOMEGUARD: THE CLAIM." The advert ends with the company's website and a phone number for making claims.

advert: Pulse smartwatch: "Your body, measured" over sleep and heart data
paragraph: This online advert for the Pulse smartwatch shows a woman sleeping, running and working at a desk, while numbers and graphs float around her body. Her heart rate, sleep score, steps and stress level are all displayed in bright blue. Each number changes constantly, even while she is asleep or eating breakfast. At one point, a message appears on the watch: "Your recovery score is low. Rest today." The strapline appears in clean white letters: "Your body, measured." At the end, the advert says the watch comes with a free month of Pulse Premium, which then costs £8 a month.

advert: A £30 printer, with ink that costs £40 and works only in that model
paragraph: This online advert for the Jet 200 printer shows the small white machine on a tidy desk beside a laptop and a small green plant. Large blue letters announce, "Only £30!" Below, three smiling students happily print bright, colourful posters for a school science project. However, the product page explains in small print that the printer only works with official Jet ink cartridges, which cost £40 for a set. It also says that cartridges from other brands will be blocked by a chip inside the printer. At the bottom, the advert also offers an "ink subscription" for £6 a month.

advert: A Chinese New Year reunion: red lanterns, a whole fish, dumplings
paragraph: This TV advert for a Chinese supermarket chain shows a young woman travelling home from a big city on the night before Chinese New Year. Through the train window, red lanterns glow in every village. When she arrives, her grandmother is making dumplings at the kitchen table, and a whole steamed fish is being prepared for dinner. The room is filled with red decorations and paper cuttings of the character for "fortune". The family eat together as fireworks explode outside. The advert ends with the supermarket's logo and a short, gentle line in gold: "Home is where the table is."

advert: An influencer's "haul" of twenty items from Trendy
paragraph: In this online video, a popular fashion influencer sits on her bed surrounded by bright paper bags from Trendy. She takes out twenty items one by one, holding each one up to the camera and saying how cheap it was. "This top was only six pounds!" she says excitedly, laughing. Many of the items still have their price tags. She tries a few on and spins around happily in front of a mirror. In the caption, she lists every item with a link and a discount code. The video ends with her saying, "I'll be doing another haul next month!"

advert: SkyHop: "Carbon neutral flights", explained by a tree-planting scheme
paragraph: This online advert for SkyHop shows a plane flying through a clear blue sky above a thick green forest. The plane's tail is painted with a large green leaf. The headline says, "Fly carbon neutral with SkyHop." Below, smaller text explains that for an extra £3 per ticket, the airline will plant trees in Scotland to "balance" the carbon from each flight. A disclaimer at the bottom of the page says that the trees will take up to forty years to absorb the carbon. The advert gives no information about how much fuel the planes actually burn on each journey.

advert: Limited "legendary" skins with a countdown and coloured flashing boxes
paragraph: In the mobile game Kingdom Clash, a pop-up advert appears while players are in the middle of a battle. It shows a glowing golden chest that shakes, sparkles and flashes with coloured light, while exciting music plays. Text says, "Legendary skins: only available for 24 hours!" A countdown timer runs beside the chest. Players cannot see what is inside until they buy it with gems, which cost real money. A small line says the chance of finding a legendary item is two per cent. The game is rated suitable for players aged twelve and over, and most players are teenagers.

advert: Bean There coffee in the style of a 1920s silent film
paragraph: This online advert for Bean There coffee is made in the style of a 1920s silent film. It is in black and white, the picture is slightly shaky, and a piano plays quick, comic music. A tired man in a black bowler hat falls asleep at his desk, then wakes up and runs through the city, dodging cars and policemen, until he reaches a Bean There café. Old-fashioned title cards appear between scenes, such as "Mr Jones needed his coffee." When he finally takes his first sip, the whole screen bursts into full colour, and modern music begins to play.

advert: Volta car alone on an open road beneath mountains
paragraph: This TV advert for the Volta car shows the car driving alone along a long, empty road through wide, green mountain valleys. There are no other vehicles, no buildings and no traffic lights. The sky is huge and blue, and the road disappears into the distance. The driver opens the window and puts her hand out into the wind. For a moment, a large eagle flies beside the car, level with the window. The only sound is quiet music and the wind. The final shot shows the car on a cliff edge at sunset, with the words, "Volta. Go further."

advert: Hollins Christmas: the mother cooks, the rest of the family relax
paragraph: This Christmas advert for Hollins supermarket shows a mother preparing the family's Christmas dinner from early morning. She peels potatoes, stuffs the turkey and makes the sauce while her husband and children play noisy board games and watch television in the next room. When the meal is ready, everyone sits down and applauds her loudly. She smiles proudly and says, "It's worth it to see their faces." Warm music plays throughout, and the kitchen is full of steam. The strapline appears at the end: "Hollins. Making Christmas magic, together." In the advert, the father carries the turkey to the table.

advert: A luxury handbag advert remade to show the worker who sewed it
paragraph: This poster by a charity that campaigns for factory workers' rights looks almost exactly like a luxury advert for Maison Noir handbags. It uses the same plain white background, the same elegant gold font and the same type of large, glossy photograph. However, instead of a model, the person holding the handbag is a tired young woman in a factory, surrounded by rows of sewing machines. The slogan has been changed from "Only 100 made" to "Made by hands you'll never see." At the bottom, a line says that the worker earned less than the cost of the bag's zip.

techniques: commodification (self-care); hierarchy of needs; direct address
paragraph: This social media advert for Bliss bath bombs shows a young woman sinking into a bath full of pink and purple bubbles. Candles are burning around the bath, and her phone is switched off on a towel. Soft piano music plays, and she closes her eyes. The caption says, "You deserve this. Self-care starts at £6." Below, a voiceover says, "Because looking after yourself isn't selfish." The advert offers a box of twelve bath bombs as a "self-care subscription" that arrives every month. It appears mainly on Sunday evenings, when many young people are feeling stressed about the week ahead.

advert: Autoplay starts the next episode; the cancel button is hidden in the settings
techniques: dark patterns; uses and gratifications (escapism); small print
paragraph: This streaming service has a homepage that automatically begins playing a trailer as soon as the user arrives. When an episode ends, the next one starts after just five seconds, with a countdown in the corner of the screen. The service describes itself as "endless stories for every mood". Cancelling the subscription requires the user to find a small link at the bottom of the account settings page, then answer three questions and click through two screens that ask, "Are you sure you want to miss out?" The free trial ends automatically after seven days, and payment begins without warning.

advert: Glacier water: an ice-blue plastic bottle and "Pure as nature"
paragraph: This billboard for Glacier water shows a plastic bottle standing on a large block of blue ice in front of snowy mountains. The bottle is clear and covered in cold drops of water, and the label is pale blue with a drawing of a mountain peak. The slogan says, "Pure as nature." In smaller letters, the billboard says, "Sourced from the Alps." There is no mention of the plastic bottle itself, what happens to it afterwards, or how far it travels to reach the shops. The billboard stands beside a motorway in a city two thousand kilometres from the Alps.

advert: Volley sportswear: women in their seventies run a marathon
paragraph: This TV advert for Volley sportswear follows a group of women in their seventies training for a marathon. They run together through a city park on cold, dark mornings, stretch on park benches and laugh about their sore knees and backs. One woman is seen collecting her granddaughter from school, still in her running clothes, with a medal around her neck. On race day, they cross the finish line together, holding hands. There are no young models in the advert. The final screen shows the women's ages, from 71 to 79, followed by the strapline, "Volley. Start whenever you want."

advert: Kite phone trade-in: "Your old phone is history"
paragraph: This poster for Kite phones shows an old, scratched phone lying in a museum display case, as if it were an ancient object. A small label beside it reads, "Kite 5, 2023." The lighting is dim, and the glass is slightly dusty. Next to the case, there is a photograph of the shiny, slim new Kite 8. The strapline says, "Your old phone is history." Below, smaller text offers up to £200 off when customers trade in their old phone. The poster appears in train stations and shopping centres across the country, two years after the Kite 5 was released.

advert: Maison Noir: a handbag covered in its own logo pattern
paragraph: This magazine advert for Maison Noir shows a young woman walking out of a famous luxury hotel in Paris, carrying a handbag covered in the brand's own logo: a repeated pattern of two gold letters, M and N. Her clothes are simple and black, so the bag is the only thing with a pattern. On the street, a photographer is taking her picture, and two other women turn to look at the bag as she passes. The only text is the brand's name in thin gold letters. The bag costs £2,800, but the price is not shown in the advert.

advert: A spinning prize wheel appears every time the app opens
paragraph: Every time a user opens the Bargain Hunt shopping app, a colourful prize wheel appears before they can see anything else. The wheel spins with flashing lights and cheerful sounds, and it always stops on a discount, such as 30% off, which is only valid for the next fifteen minutes. A countdown starts immediately. To close the wheel, the user must tap a tiny grey cross in the corner. Many of the discounts only apply if the user spends more than £40. Push notifications are sent to the user every evening, reminding users that their prizes are about to expire.

advert: Surge energy drink: fifteen seconds from yawn to triumph
techniques: AIDA model; hyperbole; call to action
paragraph: This fifteen-second TV advert for Surge energy drink begins with a close-up of a student yawning at a library desk covered in books, notes and empty coffee cups. A deep voice says, "Exam season?" She opens a can of Surge, and electric blue lightning bolts suddenly appear around her head, while dramatic music starts. In seconds, she is typing at lightning speed, answering exam questions, and then running out of the exam hall with her arms in the air. The voice says, "Surge. Unleash your inner genius." The final frame shows the blue can and the words, "Grab yours today."

advert: A famous Renaissance portrait holding a Tasty Burger
paragraph: This poster for Tasty Burger shows a famous Renaissance portrait of a woman with a mysterious smile. The painting looks exactly like the original, with the same dark background, soft light and folded hands. However, instead of resting her hands, she is now holding a large Tasty Burger, and a small amount of ketchup is on the side of her mouth. The caption says, "Now we know why she's smiling." The brand's logo appears once, in the corner, in the same gold as the old painting's frame. The poster is displayed in metro stations near the city's main art gallery.

advert: A perfect family under a perfect tree, surrounded by piles of presents
paragraph: This Christmas TV advert for a department store shows a family waking up on Christmas morning. The children run downstairs to find a huge, perfectly decorated tree surrounded by piles of beautifully wrapped presents. They open new phones, bikes, games consoles and designer clothes. Snow falls outside the window of their large, warm living room. Everyone is laughing and hugging, and nobody is shown without a gift. A voiceover says, "Give them the Christmas they deserve." The advert then shows a list of prices for each gift and offers a payment plan to "spread the cost into the new year".

techniques: uses and gratifications (information); mode of address; strapline
paragraph: This online advert for the NowNews app shows a young man standing on a crowded metro carriage. While everyone around him looks bored or tired, his phone buzzes with a notification: "Breaking: election results in." He reads it quickly, smiles and puts his phone back in his pocket. Later, at work, his colleagues in the office are amazed that he already knows the news. The strapline appears on screen: "NowNews. Know first." The advert ends by explaining that the app sends alerts within seconds of a story breaking, and that users can choose topics such as sport, business and technology.

advert: Bolt e-scooters: "Zero emissions" on green leaves
paragraph: This poster for Bolt e-scooters shows a scooter parked on a city street that has been covered in green leaves and grass, like a forest. Bright flowers grow around the wheels, and butterflies and small birds fly above it in the sunshine. The headline says, "Zero emissions. Zero guilt." The colour palette is almost entirely green. Small white text at the very bottom says that the scooters produce no exhaust fumes. However, the poster does not mention the batteries, the diesel vans that collect and charge the scooters every night, or how long each scooter lasts before it is replaced.

advert: A flash mob freezes in place for "Buy Nothing Day"
paragraph: On the busiest shopping day of the year, a group of about fifty ordinary-looking people enter a large, crowded shopping centre at midday. Suddenly, at exactly the same moment, they all freeze in place: some holding empty shopping bags, others with their hands reaching towards shop windows. They stay completely still for five minutes while shoppers stare and film them on their phones. Then they unfold banners that read, "Buy Nothing Day: what do you really need?" and walk out together in silence. Videos of the event are shared widely online, and several news websites report on it that evening.

This online advert for the FitTrack fitness app shows a young woman running on a treadmill late at night, looking exhausted. On her phone screen, a picture of a pizza slowly appears as the calories she burns increase. When she reaches 800 calories, the pizza is complete, and a message says, "Well done! You've earned your dinner." The strapline appears: "FitTrack. Earn it." Every person who appears in the advert, including the people in the background of the gym, is very slim and toned. The advert ends with an offer of a free seven-day trial and then £9.99 a month.

advert: Restaurant dishes photographed for sharing, with the restaurant tagged
techniques: conspicuous consumption; uses and gratifications (identity); aspirational
paragraph: This social media post by an expensive restaurant in Shanghai shows a dish of tiny, colourful vegetables arranged like a painting on a large black plate. Small pieces of gold leaf have been placed on top, and a single flower lies at the edge of the plate. The photo is taken from directly above, with perfect lighting. A diner's hand holds a phone over the plate, ready to take a photograph. The caption says, "Made to be shared." The restaurant tags every customer who posts a photo of their meal and gives them a free dessert on their next visit.

advert: Purity filtered tap water sold in a heavy glass bottle
paragraph: This magazine advert for Purity water shows a tall, heavy glass bottle with a silver cap on a white marble table. Next to it, a single crystal glass is filled with water and a thin slice of lemon. The label describes the water as "carefully filtered and mineral-balanced for the modern palate". The bottle costs £8 in restaurants, where it is served by waiters in white gloves. In very small print at the bottom of the page, the advert admits that the water comes from the city's ordinary public water supply, which is then filtered and bottled in a factory.

advert: Fairway Bank app in the style of a 1980s video game
paragraph: This online advert for the Fairway Bank app looks like a video game from the 1980s. The graphics are made of large pixels, and a cheerful, simple electronic tune plays in the background. A small pixel character jumps over obstacles labelled "fees", "debt" and "paperwork", collecting gold coins as he runs. When he reaches the end of the level, the words "Savings unlocked!" flash on the screen. The final screen changes to a modern photograph of a smiling woman in her late thirties using the app on her phone. The music stops, and the advert ends with the bank's logo.

A social media post shows a father making breakfast for his two children. He pours Sunny Days orange juice into three glasses while one child cuts toast. The caption says, “Start together.” The father is wearing an old T-shirt, and the kitchen looks like an ordinary family home.

Before a cinema film, a short advert shows a woman squeezing oranges by hand. She pours the juice into a clear bottle and gives it to a friend at a picnic. Soft music plays. The brand name appears on the bottle with the words “Made fresh each morning.”

A large billboard shows a boy in his school uniform eating cereal at the kitchen table. His mother sits beside him with her own bowl. Both are smiling. The cereal box is large in the corner, and the words “Ready for your day” appear across the top.

In a short online video, a man opens a box of chocolates at home. He gives the first piece to his mother, who laughs and asks for another. The chocolates sit in a black box with a gold ribbon. The final screen says, “For someone special.”

A billboard beside a bus stop shows a young woman eating noodles after a late shift at a shop. She still wears her work name badge. Steam rises from the bowl. The words “Dinner in three minutes” are big enough to read from across the road.

A website banner shows two friends preparing a meal together. One cuts vegetables while the other reads the recipe card from a meal kit. A picture of the finished dinner is beside them. A green button says “Choose your box,” and a smaller line shows the price.

Before a cinema film, an advert shows a supermarket worker making coffee in the staff room. She passes a cup to a colleague who has just arrived. They talk while the kettle cools. The packet appears on the table, followed by the words “A good start for everyone.”

In a podcast advert, the host speaks about a small coffee shop she visited. She describes the smell of the beans and says that the owner remembers her name. We hear a cup being put on a table. At the end, she reads the speciality coffee brand’s website address.

An online video follows a girl playing basketball with friends. She misses a shot, drinks from a sports bottle and tries again. Her team cheers when the ball goes in. A fast beat plays as the bottle turns towards the camera. The final words are “Keep playing.”

In a radio advert, we hear shoes on a long path and someone breathing hard. A woman asks her walking partner if he has water. He opens a bottle and gives it to her. A voice then names the bottled water brand and says, “Take it with you.”

A podcast host describes the everyday watch she wears to work. She says she can read its large numbers when her hands are full. We hear a bus door close as she talks about getting to school on time. The brand name and shop address come at the end.

A black and gold billboard shows a man alone on a yacht. He wears a dark suit and looks at a luxury watch on his wrist. The watch is bright, but his face is in shadow. The words “Your time has come” appear beside the brand name. No price is shown.

An online video shows a child putting on school trainers without help. The shoes have wide straps. She runs to meet her friends at the school gate, then stops to tie one friend’s loose lace. The final shot shows the trainers in three colours with the words “Ready every morning.”

Before a film at the cinema, a designer trainer advert shows a dancer practising alone in a large, empty studio. She repeats the same move until she gets it right. The trainers are shown close up when her feet land. A deep voice says, “Make your own mark.”

A sponsored social post shows an older woman walking her dog in heavy rain. Water runs off her waterproof coat, but the shirt under it stays dry. She smiles at another dog walker. The caption says, “Rain is still a good day,” with a link to three coat colours.

A radio advert begins with music and the sound of people entering a party. A woman asks who designed a guest’s coat. The guest gives the designer’s name, and the room becomes quiet for a moment. A voice says the coat is available by appointment at one city shop.

Before a cinema film, a basic handbag advert shows a woman leaving home with a bag full of books. At work, she takes out a lunch box. Later, she carries the same bag to the park. The final shot shows its price beside the words “One bag for your day.”

An online video shows a designer handbag being made. A worker cuts the leather, another sews the handle, and a woman checks the finished bag in a mirror. She walks into a gallery opening. There is no voiceover. The brand name appears in small letters on a white screen.

A billboard shows a teenager spraying an everyday fragrance before meeting friends in the park. The friends wave when he arrives. The bottle stands beside him in the picture. Bright colours surround the words “Feel ready to go,” and a small price appears below the bottle.

A podcast advert begins with the host describing the smell of flowers in her grandmother’s garden. She says a luxury perfume reminds her of that place. Soft piano music plays behind her voice. She names the perfume and says it can be tried at a small number of shops.

A poster inside a train shows a student holding a budget smartphone and checking the next stop. The screen is bright and easy to see. Another student beside him looks at the same map. The price is in large letters, with the words “Everything you need to get there.”

A billboard shows a woman standing on a city roof at night. She holds a flagship phone towards the lights below. The camera lenses are large in the picture. The words “See more after dark” sit beside a photograph she has taken. No price appears on the board.

In a television advert for a language app, a new student says “hello” to a neighbour in another language. At first she speaks slowly. The neighbour smiles and answers. A phone screen shows a short lesson, then the words “Five minutes a day” and a green download button.

A website banner for gaming headphones shows two friends playing a game in different homes. One speaks into the microphone, and the other laughs before moving her character. Bright lines connect their screens. A button below the picture says “Hear your team,” beside the headphones and their price.

A radio advert begins with traffic, a barking dog and a loud train. The sounds grow softer as a man puts on premium noise-cancelling headphones. We then hear him say, “Now I can think.” A calm voice names the brand and tells listeners where to try the headphones.

A podcast host describes how her children use a family tablet. One watches a drawing lesson while the other reads a story. She says they have separate profiles, so each child sees their own work. The host then gives the tablet’s name and a link to its website.

A radio advert begins with a camera clicking three times. A woman describes taking photographs of a dancer on a dark stage. She says she can still see the dancer’s face clearly. The professional camera’s name follows, along with an invitation to try it at a specialist shop.

A sponsored social post shows a middle-aged man walking up stairs at work. His fitness tracker counts each step. In the next picture, his daughter joins him for a walk after dinner. The caption says, “Every step belongs to you,” and invites viewers to set a daily goal.

A poster on a station platform shows a woman checking the home security app on her phone. On the screen, a camera shows her front door and a parcel beside it. The train arrives behind her. The words “See home from anywhere” sit above a picture of the camera.

A magazine advert shows a girl using an entry-level laptop at a small desk. She is making a poster for her school club. The laptop screen is large in the picture, and the price is printed below it. The line “Make your first big idea” appears at the top.

A poster inside a bus shows a family car parked beside a football field. A mother takes a ball from the boot while her son helps his younger sister out. There are bags and coats in the car. The poster says, “Room for every Saturday,” with a price at the bottom.

A podcast host describes arriving at a hotel in a luxury car. She speaks about the quiet ride and the driver opening the door for her. We hear the door close softly. The brand name comes at the end, followed by an invitation to book a private test drive.

In a television advert, a woman rides a city bicycle to the market. She puts vegetables in a basket at the front. On the way home, she stops to talk to a neighbour. The bike stands beside them. The words “Your town, your way” appear with the shop’s name.

A television advert shows a racing cyclist training before sunrise. Her coach waits at the top of a hill with a stopwatch. She reaches him, smiles and begins the climb again. The camera stays close to the bicycle’s wheels. The final screen gives the bike’s name and racing team.

An online video shows a man entering a budget hotel with two children. They put their bags down, look out at the city and make a plan for the day. The room price appears clearly on screen. A button below the video says, “Find a room near you.”

A full-page magazine advert shows a woman reading beside a private pool at a luxury hotel. A worker places a drink on her table. The sea is visible beyond the pool. The hotel name is printed in small gold letters with the words “Your time, entirely yours.”

In a radio advert, we hear a vacuum cleaner and a child asking if she can help. Her father shows her how to move it across the carpet. The sound stops, and they both laugh. A voice gives the household vacuum’s price and says it is available at local stores.

Before a cinema film, a premium robot vacuum moves through an empty home. It goes around a chair and under a bed. A woman returns from work and takes off her shoes on a clean floor. Quiet music plays. The final shot shows an app button marked “Clean while you’re out.”

A sponsored social post shows two flat-pack sofa boxes arriving at a shared flat. Three friends carry them upstairs, build the sofa and sit down to watch a film. The caption says, “Made for your first place.” A link opens a page with the price and assembly instructions.

A website banner shows a designer sofa in a large room with tall windows. An older couple sits at opposite ends while a grandchild reads between them. The sofa’s shape is shown clearly from the side. A button says, “Explore the collection,” but no price appears.

A poster inside a train shows a woman washing her hair after a morning swim. In the next picture, she sits at work with her hair dry and tidy. The shampoo bottle is beside her bag. The words “Ready for what comes next” appear above a price and shop name.

A station poster shows a close view of a woman putting a drop of premium skincare serum on her hand. She has visible lines around her eyes and smiles at the camera. The bottle stands beside her. The words “Care for the skin you live in” appear without a price.

A website banner shows a family speaking to a grandparent on a video call. The mobile data plan’s monthly price is beside the screen. One child holds up a drawing for the grandparent to see. A blue button says, “Choose your plan,” and the small print gives the data amount.

A sponsored social post shows a boy and a private tutor working at a kitchen table. He explains an answer while the tutor listens and nods. The caption says, “His ideas, his voice.” A link offers an introductory meeting, and the tutor’s qualifications appear below the photo.

A television advert shows a woman entering a gym for the first time. She looks unsure, but a trainer shows her where to put her bag and how to use a machine. Other people are exercising nearby. The words “Start where you are” appear with the monthly membership price.

A television advert for a wellness retreat opens with traffic and phone sounds. A man arrives at a quiet house in the hills and puts his phone away. He walks beside a lake with a guide. At the end, the retreat’s name and the dates of a three-day visit appear.

A website banner shows children sitting around a board game. One girl reads a card aloud while the others laugh and move their pieces. A parent sits nearby but does not play for them. The game box, age range and price appear next to a button marked “See how to play.”

A magazine advert shows a collectable toy robot inside a clear case. A young adult collector checks its number on a small card. Other numbered toys stand on a shelf behind her. The line “Complete your collection” appears beneath the product, with the release date in small print.

A magazine advert shows a family choosing a film on their television. A grandmother picks one title, and her grandson picks another. The streaming service’s logo appears on both screens. The monthly price and the words “Something for everyone tonight” sit at the bottom of the page.

A magazine advert for a premium bank account shows a woman entering an airport lounge. She carries a small suitcase and a work bag. A staff member greets her by name. The account’s monthly fee appears in small print under the words “Every journey considered.”

A banner on a cooking website shows two sisters making breakfast for their father. The older girl pours orange juice, while the younger one carries the glasses carefully to the table. Their father is still wearing his work clothes. A line beneath the picture says, “A little help makes the morning brighter.” The carton, price and a “Shop now” button appear on the right.

A billboard for cold-pressed juice shows a man leaving an early exercise class. He sits on the steps outside and drinks from a glass bottle while other people walk past with coffee. The picture uses soft morning light, and the label lists the fruit inside. The line “Take the morning slowly” appears above the bottle, but no price is printed.

In a sponsored social post, a father makes breakfast before his children wake up. He leaves three bowls of cereal at their places and puts a note beside each one. The youngest child finds a drawing of a dinosaur on hers. The caption says, “A good morning starts with knowing them.” The cereal box and a supermarket link appear below the video.

A poster inside a train shows a woman holding a box of chocolates on her way to visit an old friend. She looks at a photograph of them as teenagers on her phone. The box is wrapped in pale blue paper, and the brand name appears in silver letters. The line “For the stories you still share” sits above a small image of the chocolates.

A magazine advert for instant noodles shows a student coming home after a long evening at the library. His flatmate is already at the table, finishing an assignment. He makes two bowls and puts one beside her laptop. The page is bright and crowded, with the words “Three minutes. Two tired friends.” The price and two available flavours appear in the corner.

Before a cinema film, a meal-kit advert follows a couple preparing dinner with their teenage daughter. She takes the lead, reading the recipe and giving each adult a job. When they sit down, she asks them to taste her sauce first. The voiceover says, “Dinner is better when everyone has a part.” The box, weekly price and ordering website appear at the end.

A sponsored social post shows a supermarket cashier taking a coffee break with a colleague. They sit outside the store in ordinary uniforms, sharing biscuits from a paper bag. The post has no celebrity or perfect kitchen. Its caption says, “Good coffee for the days that start early.” The packet and price are shown clearly, followed by a link to the supermarket.

During a podcast, the host describes visiting a coffee grower and watching the beans being sorted. We hear birds and people talking behind her voice. She says the speciality coffee has a bright taste and explains how she makes it at home. The grower’s name and the brand’s website are read aloud at the end, along with the price of a trial bag.

A radio advert begins with the sounds of a school running club. Trainers hit the track, and several young people cheer each other on. One girl stops for a drink before going back to help a friend finish. The narrator says the sports drink is “for every kind of finish.” A shop name and the price of a bottle close the advert.

Before a cinema film, a bottled-water advert follows a night worker leaving a hospital as the sun rises. She drinks from a bottle while waiting for a bus and smiles when her son sends her a message. There is little dialogue. The music grows warmer as the bus arrives, and the final screen shows the bottle with the words “Take care of your day.”

A sponsored post shows an everyday watch on the wrists of three people. A chef checks it before opening a café, a parent checks it outside a school, and a teenager checks it before a bus arrives. Each is shown doing an ordinary task. The caption reads, “Time for the things you do.” The watch’s price and three strap colours appear below.

A magazine advert shows a woman in a tailored suit standing alone in an empty concert hall. She checks a luxury watch before stepping onto the stage to conduct an orchestra. The audience has not arrived yet. Gold light falls on the watch, while her face stays partly in shadow. The line “Before they see you” appears above the brand name, with no price.

Before a cinema film, an advert follows two children walking to school in the same style of trainers. One child runs ahead, while the other moves more slowly with a walking aid. They meet at the school gate and compare the colours of their shoes. The line “Different mornings. Same way in” appears beside the trainers, their price and the shop name.

A podcast host describes watching a street dancer practise for a performance. She says the dancer wore designer trainers and kept repeating a difficult step after everyone else had left. A short recording of the music plays beneath the story. The host then names the designer and gives the date when the limited shoes become available. The price is mentioned at the end.

In an online video, a father and daughter walk to school through heavy rain. The daughter wears a waterproof coat, but the father has only an umbrella that keeps turning inside out. They laugh when she offers him her hood. At the gate, she takes off the coat and shows that her uniform is dry. The video ends with three sizes and a clear price.

A billboard shows a designer coat hanging on the back of a chair in an empty theatre. Beyond it, an actor stands on stage during a rehearsal. The coat’s red lining is the only strong colour in the picture. The words “An entrance worth making” sit beside the brand name. There is no model wearing it and no price on the billboard.

A magazine page shows a care worker carrying a basic handbag on a bus. Inside are a lunch box, house keys, a notebook and a small gift for someone she visits. The advert uses four close pictures to show each pocket. Its main line says, “Room for the whole day.” The bag is shown in two colours, with the price printed clearly underneath.

A double-page magazine advert for a designer handbag shows an older woman and her adult daughter standing in a lift. They each carry the same style in a different colour. The daughter smiles at the mirror, while the mother looks towards the open door. The line “Never just one story” appears across the pages. The bags and brand name are shown without prices.

A social media video shows a teenage boy getting ready for his first day at a new college. He puts on an everyday fragrance, then stops at the door and checks his timetable again. A classmate later invites him to sit with a group. The caption says, “Feel ready for the first hello.” The bottle and an affordable price appear beside a shop link.

A sponsored post for a luxury perfume shows a woman getting ready for an awards dinner. She takes off her jewellery, changes into a plain black dress and adds the perfume last. The camera stays close to her hands rather than showing the other guests. The caption reads, “What remains when everything else is quiet.” The bottle appears on a dark background with no price.

In a radio advert, a man explains that he needs a phone for calls, messages and taking pictures of his grandchildren. We hear him ask a shop worker whether the budget smartphone can do those things. She answers each question plainly and gives the price. At the end, his granddaughter laughs at the first photo he sends her, and the brand name is repeated.

A television advert shows a woman recording a street musician at night on a flagship smartphone. She sends the video to her brother, who is watching from another city. The camera cuts between her bright screen and his dark living room. A voiceover says, “Bring them closer to what you see.” The phone appears in several colours, while the price is left off screen.

A banner on a travel website shows a woman arriving at a small restaurant in another country. Her phone displays a short lesson from a language app, and she orders her meal using a new phrase. The server answers and she smiles, then asks him to repeat the last word. A green “Try a free lesson” button appears below the app logo.

A radio advert begins with two friends speaking during an online game. One cannot hear the other over the noise from his room, so he puts on gaming headphones and asks her to say the plan again. We hear her voice clearly this time. The narrator names the microphone feature and gives the price, followed by a short line from the friends celebrating together.

A television advert follows a man commuting across a noisy city. On the train, he puts on premium noise-cancelling headphones, and the traffic sound fades. He can still hear an announcement when he chooses a different setting. The final shot shows him arriving at a rehearsal with his violin. The voiceover says, “Choose what gets through,” and the product name appears.

A television advert shows a family tablet being used at three different times. In the morning, a child reads a story. Later, his sister draws a map, and their grandmother joins a video call in the evening. Each person opens a separate profile. The closing screen shows the tablet beside the words “A place for everyone,” with its storage size and price below.

A podcast host describes photographing a school play with a professional camera. She could not move close to the stage, but she says the faces were still clear in her pictures. We hear the curtain open and the audience clap. She names the lens she used and explains that the camera can be tested at a local shop. The price is available online.

An online video shows a fitness tracker on the wrist of a woman who works at a desk. When it reminds her to move, she walks downstairs and meets a neighbour outside. Later, they begin taking short walks together. The screen shows steps rather than weight. At the end, a line reads, “A little movement can lead somewhere,” next to the tracker’s price.

A radio advert begins with a doorbell while a family is away. A home security camera sends an alert to the mother’s phone, and she sees a delivery driver leaving a parcel. She tells her partner that it has arrived. The narrator explains the camera and monthly service fee, then says the family can check the door from anywhere with a connection.

A website banner shows an entry-level laptop at a kitchen table. A father uses it to apply for a job, while his daughter waits to finish her school project. The two screens appear side by side to show that the laptop can handle both tasks. The price is large and a blue button says, “See what it can do.”

A television advert shows a family car outside a swimming pool. Two fathers load towels and bags into the boot while their children argue about who won the race. The children climb in, still wearing wet hair. The voiceover says, “There’s room for the whole story.” The final shot shows the number of seats, the price and the car in three colours.

In a podcast advert, the host describes being driven to a meeting in a luxury car. She remembers the quiet inside, even when the road outside was crowded. Her guest asks whether the car made her less nervous. She laughs and says it gave her time to prepare. The brand name follows, with an invitation to arrange a private test drive.

A poster in a station shows a woman cycling to work in ordinary clothes. She stops at a crossing beside people walking and takes a folded jacket from her basket. The city bicycle is shown from the side, with a map of nearby cycle paths underneath. The line “The short way across town” appears above a price and a shop address.

A racing bicycle billboard shows a rider reaching the top of a hill at dawn. Another rider, much older, is close behind her. Both are shown working hard, and neither appears to be winning. The frame and wheels are lit clearly. The words “Keep finding another climb” appear beside a team logo, but the price is not shown.

A poster inside a train shows three friends checking into a budget hotel after a concert. One carries a guitar case and another has fallen asleep on her feet. They see the room price on a screen at reception and laugh with relief. The poster says, “A bed when the music ends,” followed by a map showing the hotel near the station.

A podcast host describes a luxury hotel where a worker noticed her mother found stairs difficult. The worker showed them a room close to the lift without being asked. The host speaks about the sea view too, but returns to that small act of care. Soft music plays before the hotel name and a booking address are read aloud.

An online video for a household vacuum cleaner shows a family tidying up after a birthday party. The teenage son begins the cleaning while his father takes down decorations. A close shot follows crumbs disappearing from under a table. The child who had the birthday falls asleep on the sofa. The last screen gives the price and the words “Ready for tomorrow.”

Before a cinema film, a premium robot vacuum moves through a busy home. A woman watches it turn around her father’s walking stick rather than bumping into it. Later, he moves the chair so it can clean underneath. The camera follows both people as they make space for the machine. The advert ends with the app controls and a premium price.

A banner on a furniture website shows three flat-pack sofa boxes arriving at a small apartment. A woman and her brother build the sofa together, following pictures on a sheet. The next image shows them sitting on it with their dog between them. The words “Your place, your hands” appear next to the price and an assembly video button.

A designer sofa billboard shows a grandmother sitting with her grandson on a long green sofa. He is teaching her a card game, and the cards are spread between them. The room is simple, with a large window and almost no other furniture. The line “Space for what matters” appears in small letters beside the brand name. There is no price.

A magazine advert for shampoo shows a woman after swimming practice. She wears a team jacket and carries a bag with wet towels. In the second picture, she washes her hair at home before joining friends for dinner. The bottle stands between the images. The words “From one part of your day to the next” appear beside a clear shop price.

A website banner for premium skincare serum shows a woman in her sixties looking directly at the camera. The photograph leaves the lines on her face visible. Beside it, a close shot shows her using a small amount of serum. The line “Care that begins with your skin” sits above an ingredients link and a button to see the price.

Before a cinema film, a mobile data plan advert follows a son sending short videos to his mother while travelling. She watches him cross a bridge, then replies with a video of the family dog at home. The voiceover says, “Keep sharing the small things.” The monthly price and data limit appear on screen long enough to read.

In an online video, a private tutor meets a student who can explain an idea aloud but struggles to write it down. She listens first, then asks him to turn one sentence into a paragraph. He reads it back to her with a smile. The advert gives the tutor’s experience and lesson price at the end, followed by a booking link.

A gym membership billboard shows a woman in work clothes standing beside a weight machine. A trainer explains how to set it, and a second photograph shows her trying it herself. Other members look busy with their own exercises. The line “Nobody starts as an expert” sits above the monthly fee and the gym’s opening hours.

A poster inside a train shows a woman arriving at a wellness retreat with a suitcase and a work laptop. In the next picture, the laptop is closed while she joins a group walk. The line “Leave room for yourself” appears above the retreat’s dates. The poster also lists the cost of the three-day stay in small print.

In a radio advert for a children’s board game, we hear a child reading a card aloud. Her uncle chooses the wrong answer and everyone laughs. A voice explains that players work in teams, then gives the game’s age range and price. The sound of the final card being turned closes the advert before the brand name.

A television advert shows a collectable toy set on a shelf in a teenager’s room. She carefully opens a new figure, reads its numbered card and places it next to older ones. Her younger brother asks why she keeps the boxes. She explains which picture belongs to each figure. The advert ends with the release date and a shop list.

A poster on a station platform shows a father and daughter choosing different programmes on a streaming service. He watches a cooking show on his phone, while she watches a cartoon on a tablet. They put the screens away when their train arrives. The monthly price and number of available profiles are printed below the words “Your journey, your choice.”

An online video for a premium bank account follows a business owner arriving late at an airport. She calls the account’s travel support service and gets help changing her booking. The advert shows the call rather than a luxury lounge. The final screen lists the monthly fee and travel benefit, with a link to the full account terms.

A poster inside a train shows a young delivery worker drinking orange juice while he waits for the first service of the morning. His bicycle is beside him, and his phone displays several addresses. Across the poster, the words “A fresh start for every shift” appear in orange. The carton and a low price are printed near the route map. Other passengers are blurred behind him, so the worker and the drink are the first things commuters notice.

On another train platform, a cold-pressed juice poster shows a woman in running clothes beside a man wearing office clothes. They each hold the same glass bottle, but stand at opposite ends of the image. The label names the fruit and the date the juice was made. A narrow line of text reads, “However your day begins.” The price is absent, and the platform’s grey walls make the green bottles look especially bright.

A breakfast cereal billboard shows a mother leaving home for a night shift as her partner prepares breakfast for their son. She takes a small bowl with her while the boy sits at the table. Both adults wear work clothes, and nobody speaks in the photograph. The tagline reads, “Morning happens at different times.” A large cereal box fills the right-hand side, with a supermarket price printed below the family.

Before a cinema screening, a boxed-chocolate advert shows a father visiting his adult daughter in a new apartment. He has wrapped the chocolates himself, but the ribbon is uneven. She opens the box, recognises the brand and offers him the first piece. The camera pauses on their hands rather than their faces. Soft music plays as the words “For the moments you make” appear beside the product and an online shop address.

A podcast host describes an instant-noodle dinner she shared with her younger brother after helping him move into a student room. He had no plates, so they ate from the bowls in the kitchen box. We hear the kettle click and the two of them laughing. She reads the packet’s price and preparation time, then names the supermarket where it is sold. The story presents a cheap meal as part of a new beginning.

In a radio advert for a meal kit, a woman tells her partner she wants to cook for friends but has never made the dish on the menu. We hear vegetables being chopped while the kit’s recipe is read aloud between their jokes. The friends arrive just as the oven sounds. A narrator explains what comes in each box, states the price for two or four people and gives a website for choosing next week’s meals.

A sponsored social post for supermarket coffee shows four workers finishing different late shifts. A cleaner, a driver, a nurse and a shop worker each make a cup at home before they sleep. The pictures use warm kitchen light but leave their uniforms visible. The caption reads, “For every kind of morning,” followed by the packet price. Comments from customers describe when they drink it, and the supermarket replies with its opening times.

A speciality-coffee billboard outside an office building shows a grower standing among coffee plants, holding a small bag with his name on it.
